doc.title: Lorraine Feather interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, March 22, 2023

title: How she writes with composers: lyrics first
summary: She used to set old music, now brings lyric ideas to Russell Ferrante, Eddie Arkin and others; she compares it to Ellington and Strayhorn.

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made

blocks.x: So how does that come about? When you have a song like this and you write the lyrics, are you already singing it and establishing a melody when you get together with a pianist that you have for them, and you’re going to sing it to them? Is that a fair assessment?

Well it doesn’t work that way exactly. I used to write lyrics to existing music at the beginning — old music, Fats Waller, Duke Ellington. That’s what I did for several albums. And then when I started writing with the living it changed. What I do is, I © Fillius Jazz Archive -7-

almost always I come up with a lyric idea first and I bring it to them. It’s a little different with every guy. With Russell Ferrante I might — I often will send a little phone memo of me speaking to a metronome the phrasing to the whole song. But it’s just — it’s different with everybody. But usually, like with Eddie, he’s — Russell is a virtuosic pianist of course. Eddie is a great guitar player but we usually write on piano. So it used to be that I would always go over to his home studio and he would say, “Well I have an idea for the beginning” and he’d play some changes and we’d try out some melodies on my voice. And then sometimes he’d throw it out but I’d go, “Ooh what was that change?” ‘Cause I — like those chord changes that you named, I wouldn’t know what any of them sounded like but I know what I like. And so we just kind of work through it that way. But we’ve known each other for 35 years now so we can do it on the phone pretty much. I saw him, I saw them all a week ago in L.A. and it was just fantastic. But we had already been tossing things back and forth remotely for a long time, you know when you get to know somebody so well that way. And in almost every case it’s lyrics first. And I might have a template like I’ll say, “Well what about this — I was listening to this Bach fugue when I was writing this” or this Astor Piazzolla piece or this Scott Joplin piece, and then they’ll, that might spark an idea of something around the same tempo. But it never sounds like, you know, a sound alike at all.
Talking about writing on the phone it reminds me of anecdotes I’ve heard about Ellington and Strayhorn that kind of the symbiotic relationship they had.

Yeah. Yeah it’s similar. I mean Eddie jokes because I’ve been writing recently — well like for the last — with him, Russell, Shelly, Dave Grusin — and he said, “You’re like our mutual muse” because most of those guys just at this point had not been writing songs necessarily but it’s a thing that we do together that, you know.
That producer way back with Tommy Newsom was not at all afraid to tell you that, no I don’t like that. And are you able to say that to these pianists and accompanists, that no I don’t like that?

Well I wouldn’t use those words. Gee I don’t know because they all have such a vast trove of harmonies and melodies at their disposal. And a lot of the time they’re not sure either. And if they want to tell me they don’t like something they can, or, more often it might be something very simple like, “I think this song is too long, I think that we need to repeat this phrase” — it’s just some kind of a technical issue. And we might change our minds of course.
